screens.title: Scaling Beyond In-Process Caches
screens.narratorSegment: When a system grows from a single server to many instances, the small in-process cache each application holds quickly stops working as a single source of truth. You will learn why a distributed cache — memory pooled across servers — solves duplication, inconsistent views, and wasted R A M. In this lesson we’ll connect the idea to session stores, read-heavy APIs, and offloading your database so it can focus on writes. You’ll see two common tools, Memcached and Redis, with different philosophies: Memcached favors extreme simplicity and raw speed, while Redis provides richer data structures and optional persistence. We’ll also cover two scaling patterns: sharding to increase capacity and replication to increase availability. Throughout, I’ll point out common traps like cache stampedes, over-reliance on transient data, and network latency assumptions. By the end you’ll be able to choose the right caching approach for session availability, simple fast reads, or more advanced data structures, and you’ll know the operational checks to keep a distributed cache healthy. What’s one piece of data in your app you would not store only in a cache?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Scaling Your Cache
Scaling Beyond In-Process Caches
When many app instances exist, a pooled cache prevents duplication, improves hit rates, and offloads DBs.
Shared view of data across servers: sessions, user profile caches, or rendered fragments.
Scalability and HA via sharding and replication so the cache grows with traffic.
Operational trade-offs: consistency, failure planning, and capacity monitoring are essential.

Sharding & Replication

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will explain why distributed caching matters and when the in-process cache stops scaling. You will learn to distinguish in-memory application caches from dedicated distributed systems and identify scenarios where pooled memory is required. You’ll compare two popular solutions — Memcached and Redis — and map each to real use cases like session management or rich-structure caching. Finally, you’ll understand the basic scaling patterns used by distributed caches: sharding to increase capacity and replication to increase availability, and the operational trade-offs each brings. Each objective ties directly to a design decision you will face in a system design interview: what to cache, which tool to choose, and how to handle failures gracefully. We will also touch on common mistakes such as trusting a cache as the only data copy, and practical mitigations like TTLs, locks, or stale-while-revalidate. Consider which objective matters most for your current systems and keep that in mind as we walk the examples.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Focus
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to conceptual distinctions, you will practice the operational checks that keep a distributed cache reliable. Learn to plan for failure modes by designing replication and graceful degradation so your application falls back to the database when appropriate. You will practice identifying and preventing cache stampedes using distributed locks, TTL strategies, or stale-while-revalidate patterns. Monitor capacity and plan for evictions so that running out of memory does not cause unpredictable failures. Finally, you will think through security: authenticate and authorize access to cache clusters and avoid storing sole copies of critical data in ephemeral caches. These practical skills ensure that a cache improves performance without introducing catastrophic reliability problems. screens.title: What is a Distributed Cache?
screens.narratorSegment: A distributed cache is a pooled memory layer made from multiple cache servers that act as one logical store accessible by all application instances. This definition matters because it contrasts with an in-process cache: rather than each app keeping its own independent copy, the distributed cache provides a shared view of cached objects. Think of it like a small library branch network for hot data: instead of every home owning a copy of a frequently read book, a set of local branches hold shared copies so anyone in the neighborhood can check one out quickly. Benefits include reduced memory duplication, consistent reads across servers, the ability to scale capacity independently of app instances, and the chance to offload read pressure from the primary database. A common misconception is that a distributed cache removes the need for a database; it doesn’t. Caches are transient and should never be the only copy of critical data. A concrete example: session state stored in Redis ensures a user stays logged in when requests are handled by different servers. Key takeaway: a distributed cache gives you shared memory and scaling, but you must design for failures, TTLs, and eviction policies. How would you treat session writes differently than analytics counters in this model?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › What is a Distributed Cache?
Distributed Cache — concise definition
A pooled set of cache nodes that present a single logical cache to application servers.
Why it helps
Consistent views, lower duplication, independent cache scaling, and DB offload.
Analogy
A network of local libraries holding hot items rather than every household keeping a copy.
Misconception
A cache is not the primary data store; it is transient and should have a reliable source of truth.
Key Takeaway

Use distributed caching for shared, scalable memory—but always plan fallbacks, TTLs, and eviction policies to preserve correctness.

Illustrative example
Session storage for a web app. If sessions live only in each app process, a user hitting different servers will lose their logged-in state. A shared cache keeps session tokens centrally available even as you scale app instances behind a load balancer.
Benefit: Consistency
Same session visible across servers.
Trade-off: Latency
Network calls to the cache add latency versus in-process reads.
Check your understanding
If a session must never be lost, what additional pattern should you pair with caching? Consider persistence or write-through patterns combined with replication.

screens.title: Memcached vs Redis
screens.narratorSegment: Memcached and Redis target high-speed in-memory operations but follow different philosophies that matter when you choose a cache. Memcached is a simple, multi-threaded key-value store focused on raw performance and minimal semantics: ideal for storing short-lived strings, H T M L fragments, or query results that can be regenerated. It offers no persistence and typically relies on client-side sharding libraries for partitioning. Redis, in contrast, is richer: a single-threaded instance offering many data structures — hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets — and optional persistence to disk, plus built-in replication and clustering for high availability. Use Redis when you need structured caches, persistence across restarts, or leaderboards and queues. A common misconception is that Redis is always slower because it supports more; in practice, Redis remains fast but trades single-instance throughput for richer capabilities and operational complexity when clustering. Concrete example: session data that must persist across restarts favors Redis because you can enable persistence and replication. Memcached fits where absolute simplicity and multi-threaded throughput are essential. When deciding, map your requirement for persistence, data structures, and HA to these tool differences. Which trade-off would you accept for a read-heavy page-cache?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Memcached vs Redis
Memcached
Simple multi-threaded key-value cache with no persistence and client-side sharding.
  • Data: strings only.
  • Persistence: none — data lost on restart.
  • HA: client libraries handle sharding; no built-in replication.
  • Use case: large-scale page or query result caching where regeneration is cheap.
Example (Python)
import memcache

mc = memcache.Client(['127.0.0.1:11211'])

key = 'user_profile:1'
profile = mc.get(key)
if profile:
  print('Memcached hit')
else:
  # fetch from DB and set
  mc.set(key, {'id':1,'name':'User 1'}, time=300)
Redis
Feature-rich data structure store with optional persistence and built-in replication and clustering.
  • Data: hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, and more.
  • Persistence: optional RDB snapshots or AOF logs.
  • HA: master-replica, Sentinel failover, Cluster sharding.
  • Use case: session storage, leaderboards, rate limiting, real-time analytics.
Example (Python)
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)
key = 'product:101'
details = r.hgetall(key)
if details:
  print('Redis hit')
else:
  r.hmset(key, {'id':'101','name':'Product 101'})
  r.expire(key,300)

screens.title: Memcached: mechanics and trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Memcached is deliberately minimal: it stores simple key-value pairs, runs as a multi-threaded process, and prioritizes raw throughput for read-heavy workloads. Because it lacks persistence and built-in replication, large deployments often rely on client libraries to perform consistent hashing or other sharding strategies so requests are routed to the right node. This design keeps the server lightweight and fast, but it also means that a server restart loses all cached items and that client libraries must handle node topology changes. A concrete Python example demonstrates the get-set pattern: try the cache, fall back to the database on miss, then populate the cache with a TTL. A common misconception is that Memcached's simplicity makes it always safer; in reality, the operational burden moves to the client and to capacity planning. In interviews, describe where Memcached is ideal — large-scale read caches where regeneration cost is low — and how you would recover from node failures, for example by allowing temporary higher database load or by warming new nodes proactively. What would you monitor to detect growing eviction rates early? Memcached: mechanics and trade-offs means memcached offers extreme simplicity and speed but requires external sharding and no persistence means planning for data loss on restarts.. In practical terms, simple cache semantics and client-side sharding example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Memcached Mechanics
Core semantics
Simple key-value, no persistence, multi-threaded, client-side sharding common.
1. On cache hit, return value immediately to reduce DB load.
2. On cache miss, fetch from DB, set in cache with TTL, and return.
3. If a node dies, that node's keys are lost; clients may need to re-fetch and repopulate.
Key Takeaway

Memcached is a great fit where simplicity and raw read throughput beat persistence and complex semantics.

Code walkthrough
import memcache

mc = memcache.Client(['127.0.0.1:11211'])

def get_user_profile(user_id):
  key = f"user_profile:{user_id}"
  profile = mc.get(key)
  if profile:
    print(f"Memcached Hit for {key}: {profile}")
    return profile
  else:
    print(f"Memcached Miss for {key}. Fetching from DB...")
    db_profile = {'id': user_id, 'name': f'User {user_id}'}
    mc.set(key, db_profile, time=300)
    return db_profile

get_user_profile(1)
get_user_profile(1)
Example shows the canonical read-through pattern: check cache first, fetch and populate on miss, set TTL to limit staleness.

screens.title: Redis: structures, persistence, and HA
screens.narratorSegment: Redis is more than a cache: it is an in-memory data structure store that supports hashes, lists, sorted sets, and more. This richness enables patterns like session hashes, recent-activity lists, leaderboards, and rate-limiting counters without additional application-side logic. Redis can optionally persist data to disk using snapshots or an append-only log, and it provides built-in replication and clustering for high availability. These features let you use Redis not just for ephemeral caches, but as a durable store for certain application state if you accept the operational complexity. A concrete Python example uses a hash to store product details, showing how structured caching reduces serialization work and lets you read or update fields independently. A common misconception is that Redis persistence makes it a full replacement for your primary database — it can reduce risk of complete data loss on restart, but it still has different durability and query semantics than a relational or primary data store. For session data that must survive crashes, Redis gives clear benefits; for complex relational queries, keep the primary DB. How would you balance persistence frequency and performance for your app?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Redis Deep Dive
Redis capabilities
Hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams; optional RDB/AOF persistence and master-replica replication.
Structured caches reduce serialization cost and let you update specific fields efficiently.
Persistence offers durability across restarts but requires tuning of snapshot frequency or append-only file settings.
Replication and sentinel reduce downtime but add consistency trade-offs during failover.
Key Takeaway

Redis broadens cache use cases to structured state and durable session storage, at the cost of increased operational responsibility.

Code walkthrough — hash for product
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

key = 'product:101'
details = r.hgetall(key)
if details:
  print('Redis Hit for', key, details)
else:
  db_details = {'id':'101','name':'Product 101','price':'99.99'}
  r.hmset(key, db_details)
  r.expire(key,300)
  print('Cached', key)
This pattern uses a hash so fields can be read independently and TTLs keep data fresh without complex serialization.

screens.title: Sharding with Consistent Hashing
screens.narratorSegment: Sharding divides cache data across nodes so each node holds a subset of keys, increasing total capacity and throughput. Simple modulo hashing maps a key to a node with hash(key) modulo number_of_nodes, but this causes massive remapping when nodes change. Consistent hashing instead maps keys and nodes to positions on a ring. A key is stored on the first node encountered clockwise from its point; when a node is added or removed, only keys near that node move. This minimizes data movement and avoids a full cache cold start. Implementations often use virtual nodes to balance load and client libraries or a proxy to route requests. A concrete scenario: when you add a cache node during growth, consistent hashing moves only a small fraction of keys so the rest remain hot and the backend is not overwhelmed. A common misconception is that sharding eliminates the need for replication; in practice you often shard and replicate each shard to gain both capacity and availability. Consider how you would handle a shard failure: would you rebuild from the database, or serve stale reads from replicas?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Sharding & Consistent Hashing
Sharding concept
Partition keys across nodes to scale capacity and throughput.
Modulo hashing remaps almost all keys on node count changes, causing cold starts.
Consistent hashing maps nodes and keys to a ring so only nearby keys move when nodes change.
Virtual nodes smooth load imbalances by mapping multiple points per physical node.
Example impact

Adding a node with consistent hashing moves a small percentage of keys, avoiding a sudden surge of cache misses that would hit the DB.

Process — simplified steps
1. Hash keys to points on a ring.
2. Map each node to points on the same ring (use virtual nodes for balance).
3. Assign each key to the next node clockwise.
4. On node add/remove, only adjacent ranges remap; rebalance or warm moved keys.
Think about how to migrate hot keys with minimal downtime: proactive warming or background replication reduces user impact.

screens.title: Replication and High Availability
screens.narratorSegment: Replication creates copies of the same data on different nodes to increase availability and read throughput. A common pattern is master-replica: writes go to the master, which streams changes to replicas. Reads can be served from replicas to scale read capacity. For high availability, systems use automated failover: a promoted replica becomes master if the master fails. Redis provides Sentinel or Cluster mechanisms to automate this; Memcached typically leaves replication to external systems or client-side strategies. These features help avoid data loss and reduce downtime but introduce challenges: replicas lag behind the master, creating eventual consistency windows, and failover must be orchestrated carefully to avoid split-brain or applying stale writes. A concrete operational decision is whether to allow slightly stale reads during failover or to pause serving until a consistent leader forms. In interviews, explain how you'd minimize failover time, monitor replication lag, and test promotion paths. What SLA would you set for cache failover in your service? Replication and High Availability means replicate for availability and read scaling, but account for lag, failover complexity, and consistency trade-offs during promotions.. In practical terms, master-replica setups, failover, and read scaling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Replication & HA
Master-replica pattern
Writes to master; replicas stream updates and serve reads for scale and availability.
Replicas improve read throughput and tolerate master failure through promotion.
Failover systems must detect failure, choose a replica to promote, and update clients or proxies accordingly.
Monitor replication lag to decide which replicas are safe to promote.
Key Takeaway

Replication improves availability and read scaling but requires careful failover planning and lag monitoring to maintain correctness.

Operational cards
Detect failures with health checks and heartbeat intervals.
Select replicas with low lag for promotion to avoid large inconsistency windows.
Update routing or client topology after failover to prevent writing to old masters.
Balance faster failover against the risk of split-brain by using quorum-based leader election where appropriate.

screens.title: Consistency Models and Invalidation
screens.narratorSegment: Most distributed caches choose eventual consistency because keeping every replica perfectly synchronized reduces performance. Eventual consistency means updates propagate over time; clients may read slightly stale values for a short window. For many caching use cases this is acceptable, but for critical state you must design invalidation and write patterns carefully. Common strategies include write-through (write to cache and database together), read-through (load into cache on miss), and cache invalidation via Pub/Sub so other nodes drop stale entries quickly. Another useful pattern is stale-while-revalidate: serve a slightly stale value while refreshing it in the background and using locks or a single writer to prevent many clients from rebuilding the same entry simultaneously. A misconception is that invalidation alone solves consistency — you still face network partitions and race conditions, so design TTLs and idempotent updates. Concrete example: when updating user preferences, send an invalidation message and perform a write-through to minimize the time a user sees stale settings. What invalidation approach would you pick for menu configuration that changes rarely but must be consistent quickly? Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Consistency & Invalidation
Consistency patterns
Eventual consistency is common; choose patterns to control staleness.
  • Write-through: write cache and DB together to reduce mismatch windows.
  • Read-through: cache is populated on miss automatically.
  • Invalidation via Pub/Sub: notify other clients to evict a key after update.
  • Stale-while-revalidate: serve stale while regenerating in background to prevent stampedes.
Combine approaches depending on data criticality; for very critical state prefer synchronous write-through and replication with short TTLs.
Scenario card
Menu configuration that changes rarely but must be consistent quickly: use invalidation via Pub/Sub to evict caches and a short write-through to ensure the DB reflects the change immediately. Optionally, warm caches after invalidation to avoid user-facing cold starts.
Common mistake

Relying solely on TTLs without invalidation can leave users seeing stale critical config for too long.

screens.title: Cache Stampede and Mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: A cache stampede happens when many clients simultaneously experience a cache miss for the same key, often after a TTL expiration, and all try to regenerate the cached value by hitting the database. This overwhelms the backend and defeats the purpose of the cache. Several mitigation patterns are practical. First, use distributed locks or single-writer semantics so one client regenerates and others wait or serve a stale value. Second, add jitter to TTLs across nodes so expirations are spread out rather than simultaneous. Third, implement stale-while-revalidate: continue serving an expired but acceptable value while a background refresh rebuilds the cache. Finally, consider request coalescing at the client or proxy level. A concrete example: for a heavy aggregation query, return a slightly stale result to users for a few seconds while a background job refreshes the cached aggregation under a lock. Misconception: increasing TTLs always helps; very long TTLs increase staleness and can be harmful for rapidly changing data. Which mitigation would you try first for expensive analytics queries? Mitigation patterns
Distributed lock: only one process rebuilds the value while others wait.
Stale-while-revalidate: serve stale data while refreshing in background.
Jitter TTLs: randomize expiry to avoid synchronized misses.
Request coalescing: group duplicate requests at proxy or client library.
Choose a pattern based on acceptable staleness and rebuild cost. For cheap regeneration, locks may be unnecessary; for expensive rebuilds, locks or background refresh are essential.
Scenario — heavy aggregation
An analytics aggregation takes seconds to compute. Use stale-while-revalidate so users get the last result instantly while one background worker recomputes under a lock and updates the cache when ready.
Pro tip

Instrument cache rebuilds and monitor the rate of rebuild attempts per key to detect stampede risks early.

screens.title: Operating a Distributed Cache
screens.narratorSegment: Running a distributed cache in production requires careful operational design. Start with capacity planning: monitor memory usage, eviction rates, and network bandwidth because running out of memory causes aggressive evictions and degraded hit rates. Monitor hit/miss ratios, replication lag, and failover time to understand cache health. Security matters: require authentication between clients and cache nodes and avoid sending sensitive data without encryption. Plan for graceful degradation: if the cache becomes unavailable, your application should fall back to the database without catastrophic failure. Backups and persistence settings should match your durability needs — Redis persistence can help but requires tuning to balance performance and data safety. Common mistakes include not alerting on rising evictions, assuming local caches are consistent across instances, and failing to test failover. A practical action: create dashboards for hit rate, evictions/sec, and replication lag, and run periodic failover drills to validate your recovery procedures. Which metric would you alert on first in your environment? Operating a Distributed Cache means monitor capacity and latency, secure access, and test failover paths so your cache improves performance without compromising reliability.. Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Redis Lists Lab
Pattern: bounded recent feed
LPUSH to add, LTRIM to limit size, LRANGE to read recent items.
import redis
import time

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

def add_activity(user_id, activity):
  key = f"user_activity:{user_id}"
  r.lpush(key, f"{time.time()}: {activity}")
  r.ltrim(key, 0, 9)  # keep 10 most recent

add_activity(200, 'Logged in')
add_activity(200, 'Viewed product 123')
print(r.lrange('user_activity:200', 0, 9))
Run this script to see how lpush and ltrim maintain a fixed-size feed efficiently in memory.
Scaling notes
Shard user activity keys by user ID to distribute storage and operations across cache nodes. Ensure each shard has capacity and monitor list lengths and memory per shard.
In the lab, reflect on how trimming frequency and list sizes affect latency and memory. For high write volumes consider batching or background trimming.

fullNarratorScript:
When a system grows from a single server to many instances, the small in-process cache each application holds quickly stops working as a single source of truth. You will learn why a distributed cache — memory pooled across servers — solves duplication, inconsistent views, and wasted R A M. In this lesson we’ll connect the idea to session stores, read-heavy APIs, and offloading your database so it can focus on writes. You’ll see two common tools, Memcached and Redis, with different philosophies: Memcached favors extreme simplicity and raw speed, while Redis provides richer data structures and optional persistence. We’ll also cover two scaling patterns: sharding to increase capacity and replication to increase availability. Throughout, I’ll point out common traps like cache stampedes, over-reliance on transient data, and network latency assumptions. By the end you’ll be able to choose the right caching approach for session availability, simple fast reads, or more advanced data structures, and you’ll know the operational checks to keep a distributed cache healthy. What’s one piece of data in your app you would not store only in a cache?

By the end of this chapter you will explain why distributed caching matters and when the in-process cache stops scaling. You will learn to distinguish in-memory application caches from dedicated distributed systems and identify scenarios where pooled memory is required. You’ll compare two popular solutions — Memcached and Redis — and map each to real use cases like session management or rich-structure caching. Finally, you’ll understand the basic scaling patterns used by distributed caches: sharding to increase capacity and replication to increase availability, and the operational trade-offs each brings. Each objective ties directly to a design decision you will face in a system design interview: what to cache, which tool to choose, and how to handle failures gracefully. We will also touch on common mistakes such as trusting a cache as the only data copy, and practical mitigations like TTLs, locks, or stale-while-revalidate. Consider which objective matters most for your current systems and keep that in mind as we walk the examples.

In addition to conceptual distinctions, you will practice the operational checks that keep a distributed cache reliable. Learn to plan for failure modes by designing replication and graceful degradation so your application falls back to the database when appropriate. You will practice identifying and preventing cache stampedes using distributed locks, TTL strategies, or stale-while-revalidate patterns. Monitor capacity and plan for evictions so that running out of memory does not cause unpredictable failures. Finally, you will think through security: authenticate and authorize access to cache clusters and avoid storing sole copies of critical data in ephemeral caches. These practical skills ensure that a cache improves performance without introducing catastrophic reliability problems. A brief lab will show Redis lists and hashes so you can exercise structured caching and a recent-activity feed. Which operational skill will you prioritize first in your systems?

A distributed cache is a pooled memory layer made from multiple cache servers that act as one logical store accessible by all application instances. This definition matters because it contrasts with an in-process cache: rather than each app keeping its own independent copy, the distributed cache provides a shared view of cached objects. Think of it like a small library branch network for hot data: instead of every home owning a copy of a frequently read book, a set of local branches hold shared copies so anyone in the neighborhood can check one out quickly. Benefits include reduced memory duplication, consistent reads across servers, the ability to scale capacity independently of app instances, and the chance to offload read pressure from the primary database. A common misconception is that a distributed cache removes the need for a database; it doesn’t. Caches are transient and should never be the only copy of critical data. A concrete example: session state stored in Redis ensures a user stays logged in when requests are handled by different servers. Key takeaway: a distributed cache gives you shared memory and scaling, but you must design for failures, TTLs, and eviction policies. How would you treat session writes differently than analytics counters in this model?

Memcached and Redis target high-speed in-memory operations but follow different philosophies that matter when you choose a cache. Memcached is a simple, multi-threaded key-value store focused on raw performance and minimal semantics: ideal for storing short-lived strings, H T M L fragments, or query results that can be regenerated. It offers no persistence and typically relies on client-side sharding libraries for partitioning. Redis, in contrast, is richer: a single-threaded instance offering many data structures — hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets — and optional persistence to disk, plus built-in replication and clustering for high availability. Use Redis when you need structured caches, persistence across restarts, or leaderboards and queues. A common misconception is that Redis is always slower because it supports more; in practice, Redis remains fast but trades single-instance throughput for richer capabilities and operational complexity when clustering. Concrete example: session data that must persist across restarts favors Redis because you can enable persistence and replication. Memcached fits where absolute simplicity and multi-threaded throughput are essential. When deciding, map your requirement for persistence, data structures, and HA to these tool differences. Which trade-off would you accept for a read-heavy page-cache?

Memcached is deliberately minimal: it stores simple key-value pairs, runs as a multi-threaded process, and prioritizes raw throughput for read-heavy workloads. Because it lacks persistence and built-in replication, large deployments often rely on client libraries to perform consistent hashing or other sharding strategies so requests are routed to the right node. This design keeps the server lightweight and fast, but it also means that a server restart loses all cached items and that client libraries must handle node topology changes. A concrete Python example demonstrates the get-set pattern: try the cache, fall back to the database on miss, then populate the cache with a TTL. A common misconception is that Memcached's simplicity makes it always safer; in reality, the operational burden moves to the client and to capacity planning. In interviews, describe where Memcached is ideal — large-scale read caches where regeneration cost is low — and how you would recover from node failures, for example by allowing temporary higher database load or by warming new nodes proactively. What would you monitor to detect growing eviction rates early? Memcached: mechanics and trade-offs means memcached offers extreme simplicity and speed but requires external sharding and no persistence means planning for data loss on restarts.. In practical terms, simple cache semantics and client-side sharding example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Redis is more than a cache: it is an in-memory data structure store that supports hashes, lists, sorted sets, and more. This richness enables patterns like session hashes, recent-activity lists, leaderboards, and rate-limiting counters without additional application-side logic. Redis can optionally persist data to disk using snapshots or an append-only log, and it provides built-in replication and clustering for high availability. These features let you use Redis not just for ephemeral caches, but as a durable store for certain application state if you accept the operational complexity. A concrete Python example uses a hash to store product details, showing how structured caching reduces serialization work and lets you read or update fields independently. A common misconception is that Redis persistence makes it a full replacement for your primary database — it can reduce risk of complete data loss on restart, but it still has different durability and query semantics than a relational or primary data store. For session data that must survive crashes, Redis gives clear benefits; for complex relational queries, keep the primary DB. How would you balance persistence frequency and performance for your app?

Sharding divides cache data across nodes so each node holds a subset of keys, increasing total capacity and throughput. Simple modulo hashing maps a key to a node with hash(key) modulo number_of_nodes, but this causes massive remapping when nodes change. Consistent hashing instead maps keys and nodes to positions on a ring. A key is stored on the first node encountered clockwise from its point; when a node is added or removed, only keys near that node move. This minimizes data movement and avoids a full cache cold start. Implementations often use virtual nodes to balance load and client libraries or a proxy to route requests. A concrete scenario: when you add a cache node during growth, consistent hashing moves only a small fraction of keys so the rest remain hot and the backend is not overwhelmed. A common misconception is that sharding eliminates the need for replication; in practice you often shard and replicate each shard to gain both capacity and availability. Consider how you would handle a shard failure: would you rebuild from the database, or serve stale reads from replicas?

Replication creates copies of the same data on different nodes to increase availability and read throughput. A common pattern is master-replica: writes go to the master, which streams changes to replicas. Reads can be served from replicas to scale read capacity. For high availability, systems use automated failover: a promoted replica becomes master if the master fails. Redis provides Sentinel or Cluster mechanisms to automate this; Memcached typically leaves replication to external systems or client-side strategies. These features help avoid data loss and reduce downtime but introduce challenges: replicas lag behind the master, creating eventual consistency windows, and failover must be orchestrated carefully to avoid split-brain or applying stale writes. A concrete operational decision is whether to allow slightly stale reads during failover or to pause serving until a consistent leader forms. In interviews, explain how you'd minimize failover time, monitor replication lag, and test promotion paths. What SLA would you set for cache failover in your service? Replication and High Availability means replicate for availability and read scaling, but account for lag, failover complexity, and consistency trade-offs during promotions.. In practical terms, master-replica setups, failover, and read scaling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Most distributed caches choose eventual consistency because keeping every replica perfectly synchronized reduces performance. Eventual consistency means updates propagate over time; clients may read slightly stale values for a short window. For many caching use cases this is acceptable, but for critical state you must design invalidation and write patterns carefully. Common strategies include write-through (write to cache and database together), read-through (load into cache on miss), and cache invalidation via Pub/Sub so other nodes drop stale entries quickly. Another useful pattern is stale-while-revalidate: serve a slightly stale value while refreshing it in the background and using locks or a single writer to prevent many clients from rebuilding the same entry simultaneously. A cache stampede happens when many clients simultaneously experience a cache miss for the same key, often after a TTL expiration, and all try to regenerate the cached value by hitting the database. This overwhelms the backend and defeats the purpose of the cache. Several mitigation patterns are practical. First, use distributed locks or single-writer semantics so one client regenerates and others wait or serve a stale value. Second, add jitter to TTLs across nodes so expirations are spread out rather than simultaneous. Third, implement stale-while-revalidate: continue serving an expired but acceptable value while a background refresh rebuilds the cache. Finally, consider request coalescing at the client or proxy level. A concrete example: for a heavy aggregation query, return a slightly stale result to users for a few seconds while a background job refreshes the cached aggregation under a lock. Misconception: increasing TTLs always helps; very long TTLs increase staleness and can be harmful for rapidly changing data. Which mitigation would you try first for expensive analytics queries? Running a distributed cache in production requires careful operational design. Start with capacity planning: monitor memory usage, eviction rates, and network bandwidth because running out of memory causes aggressive evictions and degraded hit rates. Monitor hit/miss ratios, replication lag, and failover time to understand cache health. Security matters: require authentication between clients and cache nodes and avoid sending sensitive data without encryption. Plan for graceful degradation: if the cache becomes unavailable, your application should fall back to the database without catastrophic failure. Backups and persistence settings should match your durability needs — Redis persistence can help but requires tuning to balance performance and data safety. Common mistakes include not alerting on rising evictions, assuming local caches are consistent across instances, and failing to test failover. Here are the most important terms to keep front of mind. First, a distributed cache pools memory across servers to present a single logical cache to all application instances. Second, Memcached is a simple, multi-threaded, in-memory key-value cache designed for raw read throughput and short-lived data without persistence. Third, Redis is an in-memory data structure store with optional persistence, built-in replication, and many data types useful for session storage, queues, and real-time counters.
